newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks seen drifting in narrow range.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks seen drifting in narrow range.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key index is expected to drift in a narrow range on Thursday due to uncertainty about currencies, an unclear outlook for the domestic economy, and bearish high-technology stocks on Wall Street, brokers said.
Expected stagnant trade in blue-chips is likely to turn the attention of participants to smaller capital stocks, they said.
On Wednesday, the 225-share Nikkei average lost 95.81 points, or 0.47 percent, to close at 20,497.85, after trading in a limited range. Its September futures finished 20 points lower at 20,580.
"We can't expect an active trade (on the first section) again today," said Kenji Karikomi, deputy general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.
"People's attention will shift to medium and small issues with some factors to trade on, and the Nikkei 225 is likely to hover about 100 points above and 150 points below yesterday's close," he said.

Investors have held back from buying leading exporters due to the recent rising trend in the yen against the dollar. Some brokers said that they wanted to stay on the sidelines until after the Group of Seven (G7) summit this weekend.
Brokers also said that weak high-tech issues in New York would cap technology stocks in Tokyo.

On Wednesday, the Dow Jones industrial average closed lower for a third straight session, down 42.07 points at 7,718.71, after two key computer companies warned of disappointing quarterly earnings, raising concerns that trouble might lie ahead for the technology sector.
Shares of the major computer software company jumped by 180 yen to end the morning at 2,750, a new high for this calendar year. Volume was 487,800 shares.
Traders said that the buying momentum was helped by demand for new software to solve the millennium bug.
Takeda Chemical Industries Ltd also rose, as pharmaceuticals are considered to be defensive stocks which are mostly unaffected by currency movements and the condition of the domestic economy.
Takeda's share price stood 60 yen higher at 3,280 at midday, after briefly hitting 3,290 yen, a new high for 1997.

Meanwhile, shares of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) fell after the Ministry of Finance announced on Wednesday that it was suspending the bank from Japanese government bond (JGB) auctions and JGB underwriting.
Furthermore, on Thursday, the Tokyo metropolitan government said it had decided to exclude DKB from its bond underwriting syndicate starting from the July issue.
DKB's shares were down 10 yen at 1,430, but off an earlier low of 1,410.
By sector, the losers were rubber, transportation equipment, textiles, machinery, and nonferrous metals.
Gainers were led by railway/bus, warehousing, fisheries, retailers, and services.
